title: CERC Adopts Tariff For SECI's 400 MW Solar Supply To Tata Steel And WBSEDCL
seo_title: CERC Sets Tariff For SECI's 400 MW Solar Deal
meta_description: CERC's 2 November 2026 order adopts tariffs for 400 MW of SECI-procured solar power supplying Tata Steel and West Bengal's WBSEDCL.
case_name: Solar Energy Corporation of India Limited, In re (tariff adoption for 400 MW solar capacity developed through Azure Power India special purpose vehicles)
citation: Petition No. 200/AT/2026, CERC order dated 2 November 2026
body: The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission adopted tariffs for 400 MW of solar capacity procured by the Solar Energy Corporation of India, in an order dated 2 November 2026 on SECI's petition under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003. The capacity, built through special purpose vehicles of Azure Power India, splits into a 50 MW block and a 350 MW block, and the power from both is contracted to flow to two buyers: Tata Steel Limited and the West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company.

Section 63 petitions of this kind are a formality in one sense and a substantive check in another. SECI does not generate the power itself; it procures it through a competitive process and resells it to distribution utilities and large industrial buyers under back-to-back agreements, so the tariff in each power sale agreement still needs the Commission's adoption before it binds the buyer. CERC's order gives that adoption for the 400 MW package, clearing the tariff that will actually appear on Tata Steel's and WBSEDCL's power bills for this supply.

Reports of the order give a tariff range of Rs. 2.42 to Rs. 2.54 per unit across the two blocks, though press accounts differ on which figure applies to the 50 MW block and which to the 350 MW block, a detail this report could not pin down from the material available and so leaves open rather than guess at. What both principal accounts agree on is that CERC also considered, and factored in, a trading margin of Rs. 0.07 per unit for SECI's role as the intermediary procurer.

The 400 MW traces back to a larger solar manufacturing-linked tender, one of the schemes under which the government has tied solar capacity awards to domestic manufacturing commitments. This is not CERC's first tariff adoption for that tender: the Commission had earlier adopted tariffs for roughly 8,900 MW under the same lineage of SECI petitions in April 2022, and a further 334 MW in November 2023, so the November 2026 order for 400 MW extends a pattern of the larger tender being cleared for supply in tranches rather than as a single block.

For West Bengal, the order matters beyond its size. WBSEDCL is one of the two confirmed offtakers, meaning part of this solar supply chain now runs through the state's own distribution utility rather than only through private industrial buyers, at a tariff the Commission has found consistent with the competitive process SECI ran to procure it. That gives the state utility a regulatorily cleared price to plan around rather than one still sitting in a disputed or pending petition.

Tata Steel's side of the arrangement sits within a broader pattern of large industrial consumers contracting directly for renewable power rather than drawing entirely from the grid or a state distribution company, a route companies increasingly prefer both for cost predictability and for the sustainability reporting that now accompanies most large manufacturing operations. Tariff adoption by CERC is what converts that commercial preference into an enforceable, regulator-sanctioned rate rather than a private arrangement resting only on the parties' contract, since a power sale agreement without an adopted tariff leaves the price open to later dispute before the very Commission that was always going to have to bless it.

What remains unsettled on the public record is the exact date each underlying power purchase and power sale agreement was executed, since press reports gave inconsistent dates for those agreements, with one account placing a power sale agreement in October 2025 and another placing the related purchase agreement in January 2026. None of those dates affects the tariff CERC adopted, so this report leaves them out rather than present a single, unverified timeline. What the order does settle, for both buyers, is the number that will now sit in their respective power cost calculations for this 400 MW tranche, whatever the paperwork trail behind it turns out to show once the fuller record becomes available.
why_it_matters: SECI's procurement route under Section 63 of the Electricity Act means large industrial buyers and state distribution utilities only get an enforceable tariff once CERC adopts it, and this order does that for 400 MW of solar supply reaching Tata Steel and West Bengal's state distribution utility. For WBSEDCL, it confirms a regulator-sanctioned price for part of its renewable portfolio. For other industrial consumers watching the solar manufacturing-linked tender, the order is a further data point on where tariffs for that tender are settling, continuing a line of adoptions that began with the much larger 2022 tranche.
card_summary: CERC's 2 November 2026 order adopts tariffs of Rs. 2.42-2.54/unit for 400 MW of SECI-procured solar capacity supplying Tata Steel and West Bengal's state distribution utility, under the solar manufacturing-linked tender.
card_tip: Industrial buyers and discoms tracking solar manufacturing-linked tender tariffs should note CERC's 400 MW adoption sits within the Rs. 2.42-2.54/unit range set across the 2022-2026 tranches.
verification_notes: The order date (2 November 2026), the petition number (200/AT/2026, confirmed against CERC's own Record of Proceedings filed at cercind.gov.in), the 400 MW split into 50 MW and 350 MW blocks developed through Azure Power India special purpose vehicles, and the two offtakers (Tata Steel Limited and the West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company) are confirmed across the SolarQuarter and Construction World reports, which are independent of each other. The Rs. 2.42-2.54 per unit tariff range and the Rs. 0.07 per unit trading margin for SECI are likewise confirmed in both reports. The two reports disagree on which tariff figure attaches to which block and on the execution dates of the underlying power purchase and power sale agreements, so none of those specific dates or the block-to-tariff mapping is stated in the body. The background reference to earlier SECI tariff adoptions (about 8,900 MW in April 2022 under Petition 286/AT/2021, and 334 MW in November 2023 under Petition 224/AT/2023) is taken from the Construction World report and corroborated against CERC's own order listings for those petition numbers. The Commission's bench composition was not stated in either report and is left unattributed rather than guessed.
